items.description: The Australian Shareholders Association supports inflation indexation but argues it doesn't address income bunching where long-term gains are realised in one year. ASA is calling for a modern averaging mechanism to be added to CGT reform.

items.title: Is inflation indexation more favourable than 50% discount for long-held assets?
items.description: The change from 50% discount to inflation indexation requires verification. For assets held for long periods, indexation may result in a larger taxable gain than the current 50% discount, depending on inflation over the holding period. This contradicts assumptions that indexation is always better.
items.suggestion: Add to fact-checks.json: Clarify that inflation indexation does not guarantee a lower CGT outcome than the 50% discount. Provide examples showing when each approach is more favourable based on inflation rates and holding period.

items.title: Will negative gearing and CGT changes actually improve housing affordability?
items.description: The government claims restricting negative gearing and CGT discounts will help housing affordability by reducing investor demand for existing stock. The Coalition calls these changes 'toxic' and claims they will harm small business and growth investors. Property industry groups are divided - REIA praises the infrastructure spending but there are warnings about impacts on investors. The factual conflict is over whether these tax reforms will reduce housing costs or primarily harm certain investor groups.
items.suggestion: Add to debates.json: Government/ALP (ABC, 9News) says reforms will address housing affordability by reducing investor demand for existing housing. Coalition (Guardian) claims changes are 'toxic' and will harm small business/growth investors, with shadow treasurer vowing to repeal if necessary.

items.title: Claim: Division 296 tax applies to super balances over $3 million
items.description: The $3 million threshold for the Division 296 tax is commonly cited in media coverage. However,ATO indicates thresholds are indexed annually, so the actual threshold for 2026-27 may differ from the commonly cited $3 million figure. Multiple sources (BDO, Heffron) reference indexed thresholds but don't state the exact 2026-27 figure. This could lead to overstatement or understatement of the threshold.
items.suggestion: Add to fact-checks.json: claim is $3m threshold, verdict is partially_true because thresholds are indexed annually and the 2026-27 threshold may be different. The indexed threshold should be verified against ATO's annual update.

items.title: Claim: New minimum 30% tax rate on capital gains from July 2027
items.description: [SOURCE URL MAY NOT CONTAIN CLAIM — verify before publishing] Headlines frequently cite a '30% minimum tax rate on capital gains' without clarifying this applies to real gains (after inflation indexation), not nominal gains. The budget.gov.au specifies 'minimum 30 per cent tax on gains from 1 July 2027' but this represents the floor rate on actual capital gains after accounting for inflation. Someone paying tax on a $100,000 gain might pay 30% on $40,000 (real gain) rather than on $100,000. The headline rate can be misleading.
items.suggestion: Add to fact-checks.json: claim is 30% minimum CGT rate applies to all gains, verdict is partially_true because the 30% minimum applies to real capital gains (after inflation adjustment), not nominal gains. The effective tax on nominal gains may be significantly lower depending on inflation and holding period.
